_readme: The 13 candies on the landing grid (Figma 109:27), listed in the Figma grid order (109:27 rows 1-3); id = the image file number. image = file in public/candies/ (transparent 1024px PNG; webp + png sizes generated by `npm run images`). era = the timeline era id (content/timeline.json) whose collage shows this candy (draft placements from Figma 138:397; empty = not on the timeline). Copy (name, caption, body, year = Date of Invention, type = Candy Type) from Notion "Pick N Mix — Candy page copy (draft)" 402370035f2c8126a296f872ca896c4e, 2026-10-23 (draft, open questions there; "To confirm" types left empty); the drawer hides empty fields. Hand-edited (unlike content/candies.json, which is generated from the sheet).

candies.name: Skull candy
candies.year: 2020s (TikTok craze, 2024); exact first skull not dated
candies.body: In January 2024 a TikTok video set off a craze for Swedish candy in America. Chewy skull-shaped sweets led the way. So many people wanted them that shops in the US ran short, and some sweets were hard to find.
candies.caption: the skull that went viral

candies.name: Pastellfiskar
candies.year: Made since the 1950s (exact year not confirmed)
candies.body: Pastellfiskar means "pastel fish." Malaco, a Swedish candy company, makes these small, chewy fish. They are a firm jelly sweet, a bit like a wine gum, rather than a soft gummy. Shops list four flavors: lemon, orange, pear and berry, and there is a sour version too. In North America the same idea is sold as "Swedish Fish." Malaco also makes a black licorice fish, called Salt sill.
candies.caption: pastel fish

candies.name: Ahlgrens bilar
candies.body: Ahlgrens bilar means "Ahlgren's cars." These are chewy foam sweets, called skumgodis in Swedish, shaped like little cars in pink, green and white. Ahlgrens, a firm in the town of Gävle, first made them in 1953. The plan was to make marshmallows but the mix didn't rise. It tasted good though and so they decided to try selling them. They got their name in 1970, and Cloetta makes them today.
candies.caption: the world's best-selling car

candies.name: Cola bottles
candies.year: 1965 (Haribo, Germany); Malaco colaflaskor 1980s (exact year not confirmed)
candies.body: These small gummy sweets are shaped like the famous curved cola bottle and taste like cola. Coca Cola made a big splash with the invention of their famous glass contour cola bottle in 1915. Soon candy makers copied the taste, and even the bottle shape. Haribo, a German candy maker, has made cola bottle gummies since 1965 and calls them Happy-Cola. Malaco in Sweden began selling its own colaflaskor, Swedish for "cola bottles," in the 1980s. Some are rolled in sour sugar. Cola candies come in many different shapes, such as people, pacifiers, bottles, and more.
candies.caption: a cola bottle you can eat

candies.name: Fried egg
candies.year: 1980s bin staple (no maker or year given)
candies.body: This sweet looks just like a fried egg: a white foam base with a round yellow "yolk" in the middle. It is a foam sweet, the soft, chewy kind Swedes call skumgodis. The candy egg became a staple of the pick-and-mix bins in the 1980s. That's when, in 1985, Swedish shops were first allowed to let people scoop their own sweets from self-service bins, called lösgodis, or loose sweets.
candies.caption: an egg you can eat sunny side up

candies.name: Strawberry
candies.year: 1980s bin staple (exact year and maker unknown)
candies.body: This sweet is shaped and colored like a little red strawberry, with a strawberry taste. It is one of the staples that filled the pick-and-mix bins in the 1980s and is still there today. That decade, in 1985, Sweden's food agency first let shops sell loose sweets, called lösgodis, from self-service bins, so people could scoop exactly the sweets they wanted into a bag.
candies.caption: a strawberry from the bin

candies.name: Rambo
candies.year: 1980s bin staple (exact year and maker unknown)
candies.body: Rambo is a pick-and-mix favorite in Sweden. It is one of the staples that filled the self-service bins in the 1980s, and it is still there today. That decade, in 1985, the state food agency first let shops sell loose sweets, called lösgodis, from bins, so people could scoop their own.
candies.caption: rambo

candies.name: Pink marshmallow
candies.body: Marshmallow is made by whipping air into sugar and gelatin, so it squashes when you squeeze it. Marshmallow sweets came to Swedish candy in the 1960s, when Cloetta, one of Sweden's oldest candy companies, made its first marshmallow Santas. Pink marshmallow pieces like this one are a familiar sight in the pick-and-mix bins today.
candies.caption: pink and puffy

candies.name: Polkagris
candies.body: Polkagris is a red and white peppermint stick from Gränna, a small town in Sweden. Amalia Eriksson is thought to have been the inventor. Legend has it that she made a concoction out of peppermint, vinegar, water, and sugar one night when her daughter fell ill. As a young widow whose husband died days after her daughter was born, she needed money. In 1859 Amalia opened a bakery and sold peppermint candies there. The candy was a bestseller. It made her rich, and she died in 1923, aged 99.
candies.caption: a peppermint stick from gränna

candies.name: Djungelvrål
candies.body: Djungelvrål means "jungle roar." Malaco, the Swedish candy company, launched it in 1982. The sweets are small, soft licorice animals coated in salmiak, a salt with a sharp, salty bite. The bag holds four shapes: a monkey, a lion, a squirrel and an elephant. No one seems to know why those four were picked but a monkey is always on the bag and featured in their advertisements.
candies.caption: jungle roar

candies.name: Sura Colanappar
candies.year: 1961 (Nappar in Sweden); sour cola version date unknown
candies.body: Nappar means "pacifiers," and these gummies are shaped like the dummies babies suck on. Haribo, a German candy maker, chose them as its very first sweets sold in Sweden, in 1961. Cola became one of the favorite flavors. Today there is a sour version, Sura Colanappar, which means "sour cola pacifiers." The sweets are dusted with sour sugar, which gives them a sharp, tangy kick before the sweet cola taste comes through.
candies.caption: sour cola pacifiers

candies.name: Orange disc
candies.year: 1980s bin staple (exact year and maker unknown)
candies.body: This sweet is a round, flat orange disc with an orange taste. It is one of the bright staples that filled Sweden's pick-and-mix bins in the 1980s and still sits there today. In 1985 the state food agency first let shops sell loose sweets, called lösgodis, from self-service bins. Before that, sweets were sold from behind a counter, and you had to ask for what you wanted.
candies.caption: a slice of orange sunshine

candies.name: Cherry
candies.year: 1980s bin staple (exact year and maker unknown)
candies.body: This sweet looks like a pair of red cherries and tastes of cherry. It is one of the staples that filled Sweden's pick-and-mix bins in the 1980s, and you can still find it there today. In 1985 the state food agency first let shops set out loose sweets, called lösgodis, in self-service bins. For the first time, people could pick their own sweets instead of asking at a counter.
candies.caption: a pair of cherries
